title: The Tabernacle Raised and Filled with Glory
summary: God tells Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month and to anoint it and consecrate Aaron and his sons. Moses assembles every part exactly as commanded, and when he finishes, the cloud covers the tent and the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle so that even Moses cannot enter. From then on, the cloud by day and fire by night over the tabernacle lead Israel's travels.
story: Exodus began with Israel enslaved, building store cities for Pharaoh. It ends with Israel free, having built a dwelling for God, and with God moving in. Everything since chapter 25, and in a sense since the burning bush, has been heading toward verse 34. After the golden calf it was uncertain whether God would go with this people at all (chapter 33); now his glory fills their tent in the middle of the camp. The book closes with a view forward: the cloud will lead them on toward the land. The final problem, that Moses cannot enter, is where Leviticus begins, as the LORD calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and explains how a sinful people may draw near.
historical:
The tabernacle was raised on the first day of the first month of the second year (verse 17), almost exactly a year after the exodus, which Numbers 33:3 dates to the fifteenth day of the first month, and about nine months after Israel reached Sinai (19:1). New Year's Day is a fitting date: the flood account also marks a new beginning on the first day of the first month, when the waters had dried from the earth (Genesis 8:13). Temple dedications in the ancient Near East often culminated in the god's entrance into his new house, and the building inscriptions of Mesopotamian kings describe the deity taking up residence with great ceremony. In Exodus there is no statue to install; the invisible God comes in cloud and glory.

The scene has two great echoes in Israel's later history. When Solomon dedicated the temple in Jerusalem, about 960 BC, the cloud filled the house of the LORD so that the priests could not stand there to minister (1 Kings 8:10-11). Nearly four centuries later, shortly before the Babylonian destruction, the prophet Ezekiel saw the glory depart from that temple (Ezekiel 10 to 11), and in a later vision saw it return to a renewed temple (Ezekiel 43:1-5).
cultural:
Moses sets up the tabernacle from the inside out: the frame and tent first, then the ark with the tablets inside and the veil to screen it, then the table, lampstand, and incense altar, then the entrance curtain, the bronze altar, the basin, and finally the courtyard. He also performs priestly acts himself, burning incense, offering the first burnt and grain offerings, and washing, because Aaron and his sons have not yet been ordained. Their ordination, commanded in verses 12 to 15, is carried out in Leviticus 8. The anointing of the sanctuary and its furniture set each object apart for God's use alone.

The cloud had led Israel since they left Egypt (13:21-22) and had rested on Sinai (24:15-18). Now it rests on the tabernacle. In a desert, a cloud by day gives shade and a fire by night gives light and warmth, and in the ancient imagination clouds were the chariot and covering of the divine king. Israel's movements were now governed by God's presence: when the cloud lifted they packed up the camp, and when it stayed they stayed. Numbers 9:15-23 describes the practice in more detail.
literary: The chapter has two halves: God's command (verses 1-15) and Moses' fulfillment (verses 16-33), followed by the climax (verses 34-38). The fulfillment is marked by the refrain “just as the LORD had commanded him” (or Moses), which appears seven times (verses 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 32), matching the seven occurrences in chapter 39's account of the garments. The words “So Moses finished the work” (verse 33) echo Genesis 2:2, where God had finished the work of creation. Then the pace changes. After long lists of Moses' actions, the last five verses are about God's action alone: cloud, glory, filling. The Hebrew verb for the cloud's settling on the tent (verse 35) is shakan, the root of mishkan, tabernacle. The dwelling is finally dwelt in.

outline.t: God's command to set up the tabernacle
Anointing the tabernacle and consecrating the priests
Moses sets it all up as commanded
The cloud covers and the glory fills the tabernacle

doctrines.note: The book of Exodus ends not with Israel's achievement but with God's arrival. The whole point of the rescue from Egypt was that God might dwell among his people (29:45-46). His glory filling the tent fulfills that purpose and shows that his presence is both a gift and something no one can casually approach.

Everything is anointed and consecrated before God's glory comes. Holiness is prepared for, not presumed. Yet even after every command is kept, Moses still cannot enter the tent, a reminder that obedience alone does not close the distance between the holy God and human beings.

The cloud over the tabernacle directed when Israel moved and when it stayed. God's guidance was not a map given once but a presence followed day by day, and the people's movements were governed by it.

words.note: Shakan, to dwell or settle, used in verse 35 of the cloud resting on the tent. It is the root of mishkan, tabernacle, and later Jewish tradition drew the word Shekinah from it for God's dwelling presence. The Greek verb John uses when the Word made his dwelling among us (John 1:14) is related to the Greek word for tent.

Anan, cloud. The cloud is the visible sign of the invisible God, both revealing and concealing him. It led Israel out of Egypt, covered Sinai, and now covers the tent. It recurs at Solomon's temple and, in the New Testament, at the transfiguration and the ascension.

Male, to fill. The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (verses 34 and 35). The same verb described the Spirit filling Bezalel for the work (31:3). The God who filled the builders with skill now fills the building with himself.

Kalah, to finish or complete. So Moses finished the work (verse 33). The verb is used in Genesis 2:2 of God finishing the work of creation, and the echo is deliberate: the tabernacle is a new creation, completed and ready to be inhabited.

christ: The New Testament announces that the presence which filled the tabernacle has come in a person. John writes, “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The cloud of glory appears at the transfiguration, where a voice speaks from it (Luke 9:34-35), and a cloud receives Jesus at his ascension (Acts 1:9). At Pentecost the Spirit comes with fire and fills the house where the disciples are gathered (Acts 2:2-4), and Paul calls believers the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). The Bible's last vision completes the pattern that Exodus 40 begins: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people” (Revelation 21:3). These connections are made by the New Testament itself; they trace a single purpose, God dwelling with his people, rather than hidden codes in the text.

hard.q: Exodus places the incense altar in front of the veil, but Hebrews 9:4 seems to put it inside the Most Holy Place. Is this a contradiction?
hard.a: Exodus is clear that the gold altar of incense stood in the holy place, in front of the veil (30:6; 40:26). Hebrews 9:3-4 describes the Most Holy Place as containing the golden altar of incense and the ark. Interpreters have offered several explanations. The Greek word in Hebrews can mean either an altar of incense or a censer, and older translations such as the King James Version render it golden censer, referring perhaps to the censer the high priest carried inside on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12-13). Others note that the Greek verb Hebrews uses can mean that the inner room had the altar in the sense of its belonging to it: the incense altar stood directly before the ark, and its incense served the Most Holy Place. The Old Testament itself describes Solomon's incense altar as the altar “that belonged to the inner sanctuary” (1 Kings 6:22), though it stood outside it. Some scholars conclude that the writer of Hebrews was simply following a tradition that placed it inside. The first two explanations are held by many careful interpreters, and in any case the argument of Hebrews, that the old sanctuary pointed to Christ's entrance into heaven, does not depend on the detail.

questions: Exodus ends with God filling the tent, not with Israel reaching the promised land. Why might God's presence be a better ending than the land?
Israel set out only when the cloud lifted. How do you discern when to move and when to wait?
Even Moses could not enter the tent when God's glory filled it. How does that shape the way you think about coming into God's presence through Christ?
